lessons.title: A remote unrecorded outcome cannot change local statistics
lessons.idea: Conditional states can differ while the local state averaged over every remote outcome stays the same.
body: Let B choose a complete orthogonal projective measurement with projectors P_j. If its result is ignored, the joint state becomes ρ′_AB=Σ_j(I⊗P_j)ρ_AB(I⊗P_j). Taking the partial trace over B gives the same ρ_A as before. To see why, move the B-only factors cyclically inside the B trace, combine P_j²=P_j, and use Σ_jP_j=I. This is a partial-trace identity for operators acting on B, not a rule to cycle arbitrary A factors through the partial trace.

If a specific remote result j is recorded and selected, its probability is p_j=Tr[(I⊗P_j)ρ_AB]. The conditioned A state is Tr_B[(I⊗P_j)ρ_AB(I⊗P_j)]/p_j for p_j>0. Different selected groups can have different local states. Recombining them with weights p_j returns the original ρ_A. A zero-probability conditioning denominator is undefined.

For the antisymmetric pair, B’s z-plus result selects A’s z-minus state, while B’s x-plus result selects A’s x-minus state. Without access to B’s result record, A must average the two possible signs for whichever basis B chose. In both cases that average is I/2. Matching a selected remote group requires a classical outcome record; the choice alone does not carry a message through A’s unconditioned statistics.

lessons.title: A ladder changes one angular label at a time
lessons.idea: Angular-momentum components do not behave like three simultaneously known classical numbers.
body: Write [J_x,J_y]=iℏJ_z and its cyclic partners [J_y,J_z]=iℏJ_x and [J_z,J_x]=iℏJ_y. Reversing a commutator reverses its sign. Define J²=J_x²+J_y²+J_z² and J_±=J_x±iJ_y. The plus/minus operators are adjoints of one another, not individually Hermitian observables.

The algebra gives [J_z,J_±]=±ℏJ_± and [J²,J_±]=0. A ladder step changes the component label m by ±1 while keeping the J² eigenvalue. Also J_-J_+=J²−J_z²−ℏJ_z, which lets us calculate the norm of a raised state without guessing its shape.

A multiplet is a group of states that rotations mix only with one another. Irreducible means there is no smaller nonzero vector subspace within it that every rotation also keeps inside itself. In a finite irreducible angular multiplet, let j be the highest m. The raising norm must vanish there, giving J²=ℏ²j(j+1). The lowering norm then vanishes at m=−j. Unit steps between the endpoints require 2j to be a nonnegative integer. Thus m=−j,−j+1,…,j and there are 2j+1 states.

Choose phases so the ladder coefficients are positive real: J_±|j,m⟩=ℏ√[(j∓m)(j±m+1)]|j,m±1⟩. For ordinary orbital wavefunctions the allowed j values are integers; intrinsic-spin representations can also have half-integer j. This algebra is not a derivation of the spin–statistics theorem.

lessons.title: Build a three-state angular model explicitly
lessons.idea: Writing the basis order first prevents many sign and row-order errors.
body: Use the ordered j=1 basis (m=+1,0,−1). Then J_z=ℏ diag(1,0,−1), and J_+=√2ℏ[[0,1,0],[0,0,1],[0,0,0]]. Each column tells where its input basis vector goes. J_-=J_+†.
Combine the ladders: J_x=(J_++J_-)/2=(ℏ/√2)[[0,1,0],[1,0,1],[0,1,0]], and J_y=(J_+−J_-)/(2i)=(ℏ/√2)[[0,−i,0],[i,0,−i],[0,i,0]]. Both are Hermitian. Multiplication gives J²=2ℏ²I.

An eigenvector of one component can have several outcomes for another component. For example |x+⟩=(1/2,1/√2,1/2)ᵀ is normalized and satisfies J_x|x+⟩=ℏ|x+⟩. Its J_z probabilities are 1/4,1/2,1/4 in the stated order.

apply.answer: No. In the x+ state, the +ℏ and −ℏ outcomes each occur with probability 1/4 and cancel in the average. The zero outcome has probability 1/2. A mean value and a definite eigenvalue are different claims.

lessons.title: Rotate the preparation, not just the printed coordinates
lessons.idea: An active spatial rotation changes which directions the amplitude occupies.
body: For an active rotation matrix R, the transformed scalar spatial wavefunction is ψ_rot(r⃗)=ψ(R⁻¹r⃗). The inverse in the argument makes an old feature move to its rotated location. This is the rotational version of the argument shift used for translation.

For a small positive rotation α about z, R⁻¹ sends(x,y) to approximately(x+αy,y−αx). Expanding a smooth function gives ψ_rot≈ψ+α(y∂_x−x∂_y)ψ. This equals(I−iαL_z/ℏ)ψ for L_z=−iℏ(x∂_y−y∂_x). It checks both the generator and its sign.

A useful normalized angular pair is Y_x=√(3/(4π))sinθ cosφ and Y_y=√(3/(4π))sinθ sinφ. They have zero mutual overlap over solid angle. Rotating Y_x by α about z gives cosα Y_x+sinα Y_y. These are amplitudes over directions, not little paths.

An intrinsic spin also changes under rotations, but its internal components are not obtained by differentiating a scalar position wavefunction. A full particle with both spatial and spin degrees of freedom uses the appropriate actions on both factors.

lessons.title: A finite rotation mixes angular component labels
lessons.idea: The matrix exponential describes the whole turn, not just its first small step.
body: In the j=1 basis (m=+1,0,−1), use U_y(α)=exp(−iαJ_y/ℏ). Since J_y/ℏ has eigenvalues+1,0,−1, its exponential can be obtained from the three spectral projectors. Write c=cosα and s=sinα for compact entries.

The resulting real matrix is [[(1+c)/2,−s/√2,(1−c)/2],[s/√2,c,−s/√2],[(1−c)/2,s/√2,(1+c)/2]]. It is orthogonal and therefore unitary. Its derivative at α=0 equals−iJ_y/ℏ, confirming the signs against the generator.

Apply it to the highest-weight input(1,0,0)ᵀ. The output is((1+c)/2,s/√2,(1−c)/2)ᵀ. The three J_z probabilities are the squares of those real coefficients. The J² value stays2ℏ² because rotations remain inside the same j multiplet.

lessons.title: A mean angular vector is shorter than the J² scale
lessons.idea: The squared mean and the mean square answer different questions.
body: For the highest-weight state |j,j⟩, ⟨J_z⟩=jℏ and its z variance is zero. Rotational symmetry about z makes the x and y means zero and their variances equal. Since ⟨J²⟩=j(j+1)ℏ², each transverse variance is jℏ²/2.

Rotate that preparation by α about y. Its mean becomes jℏ(sinα,0,cosα). The variances are σ_x²=(jℏ²/2)cos²α, σ_y²=jℏ²/2 and σ_z²=(jℏ²/2)sin²α. These follow by rotating the centred components, not by assigning sharp classical components to each run.

The mean-vector squared length is j²ℏ², while ⟨J²⟩=j(j+1)ℏ². Their difference equals the sum of component variances, jℏ². For x and y, the uncertainty product is σ_xσ_y=(jℏ²/2)|cosα|, equal to(ℏ/2)|⟨J_z⟩| for this prepared family.

The vector of means is a summary of repeated measurements, not three simultaneously sharp outcomes. σ_x²,σ_y²,σ_z²,ℏ: Component variances and reduced Planck constant ((J·s)²; ℏ:J·s). Standard deviations σ are the nonnegative square roots of variances. lessons.title: Add operators before adding angular labels
lessons.idea: The total squared angular momentum contains a correlation term.
body: For two distinguishable angular systems, define J_i=J₁_i⊗I₂+I₁⊗J₂_i for i=x,y,z. Operators on different factors commute. Using that fact and each factor’s angular algebra shows that the total components obey the same cyclic commutators.
The square is J²=J₁²+J₂²+2J₁·J₂, with identity factors understood. Therefore J₁·J₂=(J²−J₁²−J₂²)/2. Adding squared magnitudes without the cross term would lose information about the joint state.

The uncoupled basis labels individual j₁,m₁,j₂,m₂. The coupled basis labels j₁,j₂ and total j,M, with M=m₁+m₂. The allowed total j values run from |j₁−j₂| to j₁+j₂ in unit steps. We state this finite-representation addition rule and construct small cases next rather than claiming a general coefficient-table derivation.

J² and J_z can be diagonal together with J₁²,J₂². Individual component labels m₁,m₂ are not generally sharp in that coupled basis. Basis choice changes which compatible labels are explicit, not the dimension of the product space.

The first subsystem index runs slower in the product-basis order used here. j₁,j₂,j,M,m₁,m₂: Subsystem/total multiplet and component labels (no unit). Total J_z eigenvalue is ℏM, not M alone. lessons.title: Construct the four states of two spin-one-half systems
lessons.idea: A total component of zero does not determine the total squared angular momentum.
body: Use |+⟩ and|−⟩ for each subsystem’s S_z=±ℏ/2 states. The ordered product basis is(|++⟩,|+−⟩,|−+⟩,|−−⟩). The highest total component M=1 has the unique state |++⟩; it belongs to total j=1.
Applying the total lowering operator givesℏ(|−+⟩+|+−⟩). Dividing by its norm √2ℏ produces|1,0⟩=(|+−⟩+|−+⟩)/√2. Lower once more to obtain|1,−1⟩=|−−⟩. These three j=1 states are the triplet.
The remaining orthogonal state is|0,0⟩=(|+−⟩−|−+⟩)/√2. Both total raising and lowering annihilate it, and J_z also gives zero; therefore J² gives zero. This single j=0 state is the singlet.

The singlet is antisymmetric under exchanging the two spin factors, while the triplet states are symmetric. At this stage the factors may be distinguishable systems; the separate identical-particle module will impose symmetry on a complete spatial-and-spin state.

lessons.title: Construct an unequal-spin pair instead of memorizing coefficients
lessons.idea: Lowering and orthogonality determine the small-case basis overlaps.
body: Combine j₁=1 with j₂=1/2. Write|m₁,m₂⟩ for the product states and|j,M⟩ for coupled states, with fixed j₁,j₂ understood. The unique highest state is|3/2,3/2⟩=|1,+1/2⟩.
The total lowering operator produces√2ℏ|0,+1/2⟩+ℏ|1,−1/2⟩. The coupled lowering coefficient is√3ℏ, so|3/2,1/2⟩=√(2/3)|0,+1/2⟩+√(1/3)|1,−1/2⟩.

In this two-dimensional M=1/2 subspace, a normalized orthogonal vector is|1/2,1/2⟩=√(1/3)|0,+1/2⟩−√(2/3)|1,−1/2⟩. Raising it gives zero, verifying that it is the highest state of the j=1/2 multiplet. This choice fixes an overall phase convention for that multiplet.

The coefficients connecting these bases are called Clebsch–Gordan coefficients. They are amplitudes, not probabilities; their squared magnitudes give the weights in an appropriate basis measurement. An overall sign for an entire coupled eigenvector is conventional, but relative signs within it matter.

lessons.title: Conditioning on total angular momentum changes later component chances
lessons.idea: A basis expansion is not the same as an actual measurement update.
body: Use the j₁=1,j₂=1/2 pair and prepare the product|0,+1/2⟩. It expands as√(2/3)|3/2,1/2⟩+√(1/3)|1/2,1/2⟩. This equation describes one preparation in two bases; no measurement has happened yet.

An ideal total-J² measurement selects one coupled multiplet. The j=3/2 outcome has probability 2/3. Conditioned on it, the state is|3/2,1/2⟩, which has product-basis weights2/3 for|0,+1/2⟩ and 1/3 for|1,−1/2⟩.

Therefore the joint probability of first selecting j=3/2 and then finding m₁=1 is(2/3)(1/3)=2/9. Without the intervening total-J² measurement, the initial product state had m₁=0 certainly. Conditioning changed the later preparation.

The total component M remains1/2 throughout these selected branches, but total j and individual m₁ are different observable labels. They cannot all be treated as fixed classical labels of the original state.

Component values include a factorℏ. p(A|B): Conditional probability of later A after recorded B (no unit). This differs from the unconditional joint probability, which also includes the chance of B. Degenerate projectors select whole eigenspaces unless extra labels are actually resolved. lessons.title: A scalar angular coupling can split a multiplet
lessons.idea: Use the total-square identity to calculate this model interaction without guessing orientations.
body: Consider H_int=λL·S/ℏ², where λ is a stated energy and L,S are orbital and spin angular operators. The factorℏ² removes the angular units, leaving energy. This is a specified effective coupling; we are not deriving atomic fine structure here.
For fixed l and s, use J=L+S. The coupled energy is E_j=(λ/2)[j(j+1)−l(l+1)−s(s+1)]. The same value occurs for all M within this rotationally invariant interaction model.
For l=1,s=1/2, j=3/2 gives E=λ/2 and j=1/2 gives E=−λ. Their signed energy difference E_(3/2)−E_(1/2)=3λ/2. If λ changes sign, the ordering reverses; the positive separation is 3|λ|/2.

These are interaction-energy shifts within the specified angular model. Other Hamiltonian terms, radial expectation values and relativistic corrections may be needed to connect λ to an actual atom. A simple angular identity does not determine a material-specific coupling constant.

Here l=1,s=1/2, so j=3/2 or1/2. The s label is not seconds. λ,H_int,E_j: Signed coupling scale, interaction Hamiltonian and shift (eV or J consistently). λ is energy here, not wavelength. Degeneracy in M follows the specified rotationally invariant model. ℏ: Reduced Planck constant (J·s). Dividing L·S byℏ² makes a dimensionless operator. lessons.title: For identical particles, labels are bookkeeping
lessons.idea: The full state must obey the appropriate exchange rule, not just its spatial sketch.
body: For two identical particles, let Π exchange every single-particle argument: position and any internal spin label. In coordinates, [ΠΨ](r₁,s₁;r₂,s₂)=Ψ(r₂,s₂;r₁,s₁). Exchanging twice returns the same function, so Π²=I.

In the ordinary three-dimensional boson/fermion framework used here, complete boson states are symmetric, ΠΨ=+Ψ, and complete fermion states are antisymmetric, ΠΨ=−Ψ. We take this statistics rule as physical input. Its connection to spin in relativistic field theory is not derived by this nonrelativistic algebra.

The labels1 and 2 identify tensor slots in the calculation, not permanent observable tags attached to two identical particles. Different species, such as an electron and proton, can be distinguished by their physical type and need not be symmetrized as one species.

A physical Hamiltonian for identical particles preserves the appropriate exchange sector. A claimed single-particle label operation that distinguishes otherwise identical particles needs a real distinguishing degree of freedom or spatial mode, not merely a renamed tensor slot.

For two 3D particles with discrete spin labels, spatial amplitudes have units m⁻³ and norm includes a spin sum plus d³r₁d³r₂. r₁,r₂,s₁,s₂: Positions and internal spin labels in the two slots (positions:m; spin labels:no unit). Both position and spin arguments are exchanged. The s labels are not elapsed time. ±1: Exchange eigenvalue (no unit). Plus describes bosons and minus fermions here. This is not a probability sign. apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does antisymmetry itself add a new classical repulsive force to the Hamiltonian?
apply.answer: No. It restricts the allowed quantum states and changes their measurement and energy statistics. Actual interactions must still be specified in the Hamiltonian. Calling the exchange rule a separate classical force confuses the state constraint with an interaction term.

lessons.title: Overlapping one-particle states change the normalization
lessons.idea: Two swapped terms are not automatically orthogonal.
body: Let u and v be normalized one-particle states, with overlap S=⟨u|v⟩. The symmetric numerator is|u,v⟩+|v,u⟩. Its norm squared has two diagonal terms equal to one and two cross terms equal to|S|², so the total is 2(1+|S|²).

The normalized boson pair is Ψ_+=(|u,v⟩+|v,u⟩)/√[2(1+|S|²)]. The familiar1/√2 coefficient applies only when u and v are orthogonal. If they are identical, the numerator and denominator both contain the factor 2, leaving the normalized product|u,u⟩.

Nonorthogonal u and v are not two mutually exclusive measurement outcomes. To calculate probabilities, choose a complete orthonormal measurement basis and expand the pair there. Do not call the overlapping-state labels independent detector bins.

Ψ_+,|u,v⟩: Symmetric normalized pair and ordered product u⊗v (no unit in the example). This is a bosonic state in the stated one-particle mode space. |0⟩,|1⟩: Orthonormal detector-mode basis (no unit). Outcome probabilities below refer to these orthogonal modes, not directly to overlapping u and v. lessons.title: Antisymmetry removes duplicate complete one-particle states
lessons.idea: The zero result is not a normalized state with a mysterious repulsive push.
body: For orthonormal complete one-particle states u and v, form Ψ_-=(|u,v⟩−|v,u⟩)/√2. In position-and-spin coordinates, this is the two-by-two Slater determinant of the single-particle amplitudes divided by √2.

Exchange the two complete particle arguments and the determinant changes sign. If the two one-particle columns are identical, the determinant vanishes. Two identical fermions therefore cannot occupy the same complete one-particle state in this description; that is the Pauli exclusion rule.

The word complete matters: a spatial orbital together with spin labels is a single-particle state. Two electrons may share a spatial orbital if their complete spin-orbital states are different. The normalization1/√2 here assumes u and v are orthonormal.

In a finite two-mode basis with u=|0⟩,v=|1⟩, the ordered coefficients are(0,1/√2,−1/√2,0). Physical occupation measurements always find one fermion in each of those modes; tensor-slot labels are not particle identity tags.

lessons.title: Combine the spatial and spin signs
lessons.idea: For two electrons, the product of the two exchange signs must be minus.
body: If a two-electron state factors into a spatial partφ and a spin partχ, exchanging complete particles exchanges both factors. Their signs multiply. A symmetric spatial factor must therefore pair with an antisymmetric spin factor, and an antisymmetric spatial factor with a symmetric spin factor.

The spin singletχ_s=(|+−⟩−|−+⟩)/√2 is antisymmetric. The three triplet states are symmetric. For orthonormal spatial orbitals a,b, spatial sums/differencesφ_±=(|a,b⟩±|b,a⟩)/√2 have the indicated signs.

When both electrons occupy the same spatial orbital a, the spatial product|a,a⟩ is symmetric. The allowed factorized spin state is then the singlet. An unantisymmetrized product|+−⟩ alone is not the required complete two-electron state.

These restrictions come from exchange symmetry, not from a claim that the singlet is always the lowest-energy choice. Interactions and occupied spatial orbitals determine the energy. More general spin-spatial states can be entangled rather than a single factorized product.

lessons.title: Count occupations of modes, not names of identical particles
lessons.idea: The list of one-particle modes must say whether spin is already included.
body: An occupation list(n₀,n₁,…) gives the number of particles in each orthonormal complete mode. Its entries sum to the fixed particle number N. Boson occupations can be0,1,2,…; fermion occupations are 0 or1 for each complete mode.

For a noninteracting Hamiltonian with one-particle energiesε_j, the total energy is E=Σ_j n_jε_j. Interactions generally change this simple sum. A mode includes any spin label, so “one fermion per mode” is not automatically “one per spatial orbital.”
With two spinless modes and N=2, bosons have three occupation lists:(2,0),(1,1),(0,2). Spinless fermions have only(1,1). Exchanging particle-slot names does not create a new occupation configuration.

If each spatial orbital instead has two orthogonal spin states, list those as separate complete modes before filling. State whether energies are degenerate and whether interactions are neglected; otherwise a lowest-energy filling claim is incomplete.

Energy reference shifts must be applied consistently. Spinless model: A model with no additional spin degeneracy in its listed modes (no unit). It is not a claim that real electrons have no spin. lessons.title: Exchange symmetry changes an interaction expectation
lessons.idea: The change comes from interference terms in an allowed state, not a new classical force.
body: Take two orthonormal spatial orbitals u,v and a real interaction W(r₁,r₂)=W(r₂,r₁). Define the direct integral J_d=∫u₁*v₂*W u₁v₂ d³r₁d³r₂ and exchange integral K_ex=∫u₁*v₂*W v₁u₂ d³r₁d³r₂. Here u₁ means u(r₁), and the six-dimensional measure means integrate over both 3D positions.

Expand the interaction expectation inφ_±=(u₁v₂±v₁u₂)/√2. The two direct terms each give J_d; the two cross terms give±K_ex. For the stated exchange-symmetric real interaction K_ex is real, so ⟨W⟩_±=J_d±K_ex.

If the one-body orbital energies areε_u andε_v, their sum is the same in these two chosen states. Thus the full energy expectations areε_u+ε_v+J_d±K_ex. The symmetric spatial state pairs with a spin singlet, and the antisymmetric spatial state with a spin triplet for electrons.

These are expectation values in the stated fixed orbitals. They are not automatically exact interacting eigenenergies or optimized ground states. The sign and size of K_ex belong to the specified interaction and orbitals; do not turn a supplied positive example into a universal ordering for arbitrary interactions.

W,J_d,K_ex,ε_u,ε_v,H: Interaction, direct/exchange integrals, one-body energies and total Hamiltonian (J or eV consistently). J_d is an energy here, not an angular-momentum operator. K_ex is not a kinetic-energy symbol. d³r₁d³r₂,φ_±: Two-position volume measure and normalized spatial pair (m⁶; φ_±:m⁻³). Star conjugates amplitudes. Orthogonality makes the pair normalization√2 valid. ±: Spatial symmetry sign (no unit). Plus means symmetric space; minus antisymmetric space. Electron spin symmetry supplies the opposite sign. lessons.title: Track a spin preparation through a turn and two filters
lessons.idea: Name the preparation again after every recorded measurement.
body: Prepare|+z⟩=(1,0)ᵀ and apply an active y rotation U_y(θ)=exp(−iθσ_y/2). The output spinor is(cos(θ/2),sin(θ/2))ᵀ. These are amplitudes; the rotation angle is θ, while the spinor uses half-angles.

Next record a successful+z projection and then a successful−x projection. The first probability is cos²(θ/2). Its conditioned state is +z, so the later−x probability is 1/2. The whole sequence has probability(1/2)cos²(θ/2).
If there is no intermediate z measurement, the −x probability is instead|[cos(θ/2)−sin(θ/2)]/√2|²=(1−sinθ)/2. The two questions describe different physical procedures, not conflicting predictions.

If the z measurement happens but its result is ignored, sum the later probabilities over both z branches. Each gives −x chance 1/2, so the unconditioned later chance is 1/2. This is distinct from selecting only the +z branch.

lessons.title: Keep coupling, detuning and time phase separate
lessons.idea: A population can change even while the energy distribution of a fixed Hamiltonian stays unchanged.
body: Use the time-independent Hamiltonian H=(Δ/2)σ_z+gσ_x in the ordered reference basis (|0⟩,|1⟩). Both Δ and the real coupling g are energies. Let d=√[(Δ/2)²+g²], so H²=d²I and the two energy eigenvalues are±d.

The exact evolution is U=cos(dt/ℏ)I−i sin(dt/ℏ)H/d for d>0. Starting in|0⟩ gives the transition probability P₁(t)=(g²/d²)sin²(dt/ℏ). A nonzero detuning reduces its maximum; changing the time phase controls where the oscillation is within that bound.

The initial energy expectation isΔ/2, and its energy-eigenstate probabilities are[1±Δ/(2d)]/2. Those weights remain constant under this H even though the reference-basis populations change. Off-diagonal coherence contributes to the energy expectation in the reference basis.

This Hamiltonian is already constant, so its exact exponential does not require a rotating-wave approximation. If it was obtained by approximating a laboratory drive, the frame definition and approximation conditions must also be supplied; the constant matrix alone does not prove that reduction valid.

lessons.title: Do not mix distinguishable subsystems with identical-particle slots
lessons.idea: First name the physical subsystems and whether an outcome record is available.
body: First consider two distinguishable spin-one-half systems A and B in ψ=√(3/4)|00⟩+i√(1/4)|11⟩. Tracing out B givesρ_A=diag(3/4,1/4). Its purity is Tr(ρ_A²)=5/8, even though the joint state is pure.

If B is measured in the plus/minus basis and the + result is recorded, that result has probability 1/2. The conditioned A state is√(3/4)|0⟩+i√(1/4)|1⟩, a pure state. If B’s result is ignored, averaging both branches restores the sameρ_A as before. Conditioning and unconditioned local statistics answer different questions.

Now consider a separate preparation of two identical electrons in the same spatial orbital. Their complete antisymmetric state has the spin singlet factor. The distinguishable-subsystem labels in the first example are not a permission to attach permanent identity tags to these identical particles.

For different spatial orbitals, an antisymmetric spatial factor pairs with a symmetric triplet spin factor. Check the full exchange sign and the stated mode definitions before applying a two-system formula. Treat the two setups as separate physical preparations.

lessons.title: Test whether the state and the question fit together
lessons.idea: A correct formula still needs a valid state, basis, domain and measurement procedure.
body: For a finite density operator, first checkρ†=ρ, Trρ=1 and nonnegative eigenvalues. Trace one alone is not enough. The probability of a projective outcome P is Tr(ρP), and the expectation of an observable A is Tr(ρA). Their units differ if A is dimensional.

Before using an angular label, check its allowed range and whether it is individual or total. Before filling modes with fermions, check whether spin is included in the mode label. Before applying a rotation or measurement, say whether it changes the preparation or only the coordinate description.

The small tests here combine earlier tools rather than certify all quantum theory. Try a fresh case, explain the result in plain words and name an assumption that would change it. Missing prerequisites are a reason to practise a specific step, not to hide the question behind notation.

General approximation methods and scattering analysis remain in Quantum III. Rigorous continuum spectral theory, general measurement maps, interacting many-body/field theory and laboratory control remain named extensions. A completion mark records your progress, not independent mastery of those areas.
lessons.terms: ρ,ρ†,Tr: Finite density matrix, its adjoint and trace (no unit). A valid state is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and trace one; the term positive semidefinite means every eigenvalue is nonnegative. A projector is not an arbitrary matrix; ideal projective families also obey completeness/orthogonality. σ_x,σ_y,σ_z: Pauli matrices in the stated zero/one basis (no unit). σ_y=[[0,−i],[i,0]]. Physical spin components areℏ/2 times these matrices. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), J joule (energy), eV electronvolt (energy), rad radian (angle). ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, in J·s or eV·s consistently. Finite-basis state coefficients, probabilities and pure-number matrices are dimensionless unless stated otherwise. Observable eigenvalues carry the observable’s units. A dagger means conjugate transpose; a star conjugates a scalar. I is the identity map. Bare arithmetic uses values in the declared units.
